case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Quiet Title Act’s 12-year filing deadline limits a federal court’s subject-matter jurisdiction or instead operates as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule (i.e., an ordinary statute of limitations).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Quiet Title Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g) (12-year deadline for bringing "[a]ny civil action under" the QTA, with an exception for actions brought by a State).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue the QTA’s 12-year deadline is not jurisdictional because Congress did not clearly state that the time bar limits subject-matter jurisdiction; under the Supreme Court’s modern clear-statement rule, time limits are presumptively nonjurisdictional and should be treated like ordinary statutes of limitations. As a result, the deadline should be addressed under Rule 12(b)(6) rather than Rule 12(b)(1), with ordinary procedural consequences (e.g., waiver/forfeiture, equitable doctrines where applicable, and merits-style pleading standards). Petitioners also contend that prior lower-court practice treating the deadline as jurisdictional improperly conflates a sovereign-immunity waiver with jurisdiction, and that labeling it jurisdictional creates unjust results in land-title disputes by requiring dismissal even when the government delays raising timeliness or when factual development is needed.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that the QTA’s 12-year deadline is jurisdictional because it is part of the statutory conditions on the government’s waiver of sovereign immunity for quiet-title suits; historically, such conditions are treated as limits on the court’s power to hear the case. The government emphasizes the QTA’s text tying the deadline to "[a]ny civil action under" the Act and the long-standing understanding in the courts of appeals that QTA timeliness is a jurisdictional prerequisite. It further contends that treating the deadline as jurisdictional protects the federal government’s strong interests in certainty and repose regarding title to federal lands and avoids exposing the United States to stale land claims.
key_precedents: Caltex Plastics, Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp., 824 F.3d 1156 (9th Cir. 2016)
Parrino v. FHP, Inc., 146 F.3d 699 (9th Cir. 1998)
Steinle v. City & Cty. of San Francisco, 919 F.3d 1154 (9th Cir. 2019)
Maya v. Centex Corp., 658 F.3d 1060 (9th Cir. 2011)
Tobar v. United States, 639 F.3d 1191 (9th Cir. 2011)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh make the best opposing point that, under Wong’s clear-statement framework, § 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless” looks like an ordinary limitations defense and lacks the familiar “no court shall have jurisdiction” formulation. But Block v. North Dakota did more than use pre-Arbaugh “jurisdictional shorthand”; it construed this specific Quiet Title Act time bar as part of a carefully delimited, exclusive waiver designed to secure repose in federal land titles, and that construction has organized QTA litigation and reliance interests for decades. Under a minimalist, institution-protective approach, Wong’s general clear-statement rule should not be read to sub silentio unsettle Block’s QTA-specific holding absent a clearer signal from Congress or an unmistakable directive from this Court. Justice Sotomayor’s fairness concerns underscore the costs of jurisdictional labeling, but those policy tradeoffs were integral to Congress’s compromise for title stability and are better addressed legislatively than by relabeling a long-settled limitation in this specialized statutory scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press that Wong’s clear-statement rule controls because § 2409a(g) lacks “no court shall have jurisdiction” language, but that modern labeling doctrine cannot override the original public meaning of a condition attached to the United States’ consent to be sued. The Act’s text makes the 12-year limit a prerequisite for “[a]ny civil action under this section,” which, in the historical understanding of sovereign-immunity waivers, defines the scope of the consent and thus the court’s lawful authority to proceed when the condition is unmet. Block v. North Dakota is therefore not mere pre-Arbaugh “shorthand,” as Justice Sotomayor suggests, but a construction of this very waiver—“no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits”—that accords with the statute’s compromise for repose in federal land titles. Even accepting Wong’s framework in general, it should not be read to silently displace a QTA-specific holding and the waiver-limiting structure Congress enacted here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that Wong/Arbaugh require an unmistakable textual jurisdictional hook and that “shall be barred unless” is ordinary limitations language—does not, to my mind, grapple with the Quiet Title Act’s distinctive structure as an exclusive, carefully delimited waiver governing land-title repose. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Block v. North Dakota was not merely pre-framework “shorthand”; it construed this specific statutory compromise and has anchored decades of settled expectations that untimely QTA suits are outside the courts’ authority to adjudicate against the United States. Justice Sotomayor is right that strict merits enforcement can often protect repose, but the jurisdictional characterization here does additional work consistent with the waiver’s design by preventing adjudication when the condition on “any civil action under this section” is unmet, rather than permitting waiver/forfeiture to expand consent. Given the unusually weighty reliance interests in stable land titles and the statute’s waiver-conditioned phrasing, I am not persuaded Wong silently displaced Block’s QTA-specific construction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance/stare decisis point—that Block specifically read this QTA deadline as leaving “no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits” and that land-title repose has structured decades of practice—is the strongest counterweight. But under Kwai Fun Wong’s clear-statement rule, we do not treat older “jurisdiction” characterizations as doing Congress’s work when the statute’s own text (§ 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless”) lacks an unmistakable link to adjudicatory power, and Justice Thomas’s waiver-condition original-meaning account cannot override that settled interpretive framework. Justice Alito is right that repose is unusually weighty here, yet that interest is fully served by strict merits enforcement (and narrow tolling consistent with Block/Beggerly) without the harsh, resource-skewing collateral consequences of jurisdictional labeling (sua sponte dismissal, nonwaivability, constrained factual development). Block and Beggerly therefore remain relevant to rigor, not to the jurisdictional classification, and nothing in my colleagues’ arguments genuinely undermines that doctrinal and practical line.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s best point is stare decisis and reliance: Block expressly said an untimely QTA claim leaves courts with “no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits,” and land-title repose is unusually weighty. But under Arbaugh/Kwai Fun Wong, we treat “jurisdictional” as a clear-text inquiry, and § 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless” (outside any jurisdiction-granting provision and without “no court shall have jurisdiction” language) does not clearly link the 12-year limit to adjudicatory power; Block’s pre–clear-statement usage cannot supply that missing statutory hook. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning account—that waiver conditions necessarily limit authority—does not fit our current framework, which expressly rejects automatic jurisdictional treatment for waiver-adjacent deadlines and instead preserves sovereign and repose interests through strict (but waivable/forfeitable) enforcement on the merits. Block and Beggerly still do important work in demanding rigor and narrow tolling, so relabeling the bar as nonjurisdictional need not disturb the stability interests Roberts and Alito emphasize.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is that Block construed this very provision, and that QTA reliance interests counsel against relabeling now; Justice Thomas adds that, as an original matter, conditions on sovereign consent necessarily define adjudicatory authority. But under our post-Arbaugh clear-statement framework—applied in Kwai Fun Wong even in the sovereign-immunity context—jurisdiction turns on what Congress clearly said, and § 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless” is the language of an ordinary time bar, not a jurisdictional withdrawal, and it appears outside any jurisdiction-granting text. Block’s “no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits” line can be preserved as a demand for strict enforcement and narrow tolling (as Justices Kagan and Barrett suggest), yet it cannot supply a jurisdictional command Congress did not write. Respect for separation of powers cuts against letting judicial characterizations and reliance interests expand or contract Article III jurisdiction without a clear statutory directive.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance/stare decisis point grounded in Block’s “no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits” language is the best argument for respondent, especially given the QTA’s repose function that Justice Alito underscores. But under our post-Arbaugh clear-statement framework as applied in Kwai Fun Wong, we do not treat time bars as jurisdictional— even in sovereign-immunity waivers—unless Congress clearly ties the deadline to adjudicatory power, and § 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless” reads like a conventional limitations provision rather than a jurisdictional withdrawal. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning view that waiver conditions inherently delimit judicial power is serious, yet Wong specifically rejects automatic jurisdictional treatment of waiver-adjacent deadlines, and Block’s pre-framework labeling cannot supply the unmistakable textual signal Wong requires. We can respect Block/Beggerly and land-title stability by enforcing the 12-year bar strictly as a merits defense, without importing the nonwaivable, sua sponte, jurisdictional consequences that our modern doctrine counsels against.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis point about Block v. North Dakota is the strongest counterweight: Block did construe this very QTA provision against the backdrop of a carefully delimited waiver and land-title repose. But under our post-Arbaugh framework, as applied in Kwai Fun Wong, the jurisdictional inquiry turns on Congress’s clear textual linkage between a rule and adjudicatory authority, and § 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless” lacks the jurisdictional formulation and placement that would satisfy that clear-statement requirement. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning account that conditions on consent necessarily limit judicial power is serious, yet Wong specifically rejected automatic “waiver-condition = jurisdictional” treatment absent clear text, and I do not read Block’s “no jurisdiction” language—issued pre-framework—as enough to supply what Congress did not say. Block and Beggerly still do substantial work in requiring strict enforcement and narrow tolling, preserving repose without importing the collateral consequences of jurisdictional labeling.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s reliance/stare decisis point about Block v. North Dakota is the most serious counterweight, but Block’s “no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits” phrasing is precisely the kind of pre-Arbaugh labeling that our clear-statement cases (as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize) refuse to treat as a substitute for Congress’s text. Section 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless” language—outside any jurisdiction-granting provision and without “no court shall have jurisdiction” wording—does not clearly make timeliness a limit on adjudicatory power even in a sovereign-immunity waiver, consistent with Kwai Fun Wong. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning view that waiver conditions necessarily delimit jurisdiction is weighty, but under current doctrine the question is what Congress clearly enacted, and we can protect land-title repose through strict (though waivable/forfeitable) enforcement without importing jurisdictional collateral consequences that undermine procedural fairness. Block and Beggerly still matter, but mainly to confirm rigor in applying the bar and skepticism about tolling—not to override the statute’s nonjurisdictional phrasing under the modern framework.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Quiet Title Act’s 12-year bar, 28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g), is written as a condition on bringing "[a]ny civil action under" the Act, and the QTA is itself the exclusive waiver of sovereign immunity for quiet-title claims against the United States—making Congress’s conditions on that waiver especially weighty. In Block v. North Dakota, 461 U.S. 273, 292 (1983), the Court stated that if the QTA limitations period barred the suit, “the courts below had no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits,” language that lower courts have long treated as controlling on the jurisdictional character of § 2409a(g). Given the reliance interests and the federal government’s strong need for repose and certainty in land title, institutional legitimacy counsels adhering to Block absent a clear directive that it was merely “mandatory” rather than jurisdictional. A narrow ruling that preserves the established understanding of the QTA’s timing condition best respects precedent and avoids unsettling a large body of federal land-title litigation practice.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Quiet Title Act provides a limited waiver of sovereign immunity, and § 2409a(g) states that “[a]ny civil action under this section” must be commenced within 12 years (with a State exception), making timeliness a textual condition on the very cause of action Congress authorized against the United States. Under the original public meaning of such waivers, conditions attached to the sovereign’s consent to be sued delimit the courts’ power to entertain the suit, not merely the parties’ procedural obligations. This Court in Block v. North Dakota treated the QTA time bar as defeating the courts’ ability to reach the merits, stating that if the claim is time-barred “the courts below had no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits,” which aligns with the understanding that failure to satisfy the statutory condition leaves no lawful basis to proceed. The modern “clear-statement” approach cannot override the statute’s text and structure as a sovereign-immunity waiver and this Court’s controlling construction of that waiver’s conditions.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Quiet Title Act’s waiver of sovereign immunity is strictly conditioned by its text, which provides that “[a]ny civil action under” the Act must be brought within 12 years, 28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g), and that timing condition should be treated as limiting the court’s power to entertain the suit. In Block v. North Dakota, the Court stated that if a QTA claim is time-barred “the courts below had no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits,” reflecting the longstanding understanding that the limitations period is a jurisdictional prerequisite tied to the waiver itself. Given the federal government’s strong interests in repose and stable title to public lands, treating § 2409a(g) as jurisdictional avoids practical consequences like waiver/forfeiture that could expose the United States to stale land claims. Whatever the force of the Court’s modern clear-statement approach in other contexts, it should not be used to dilute Congress’s conditions on a sovereign-immunity waiver in this land-title setting.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under the Court’s clear-statement rule, filing deadlines are presumptively nonjurisdictional "claim-processing rules" unless Congress clearly states otherwise, and nothing in 28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g) unmistakably speaks in jurisdictional terms. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong rejected the notion that a limitations period becomes jurisdictional merely because it appears in a statute waiving sovereign immunity; that reasoning applies here, where the QTA’s 12-year deadline is framed as a time bar for bringing an action, not as a limit on the court’s adjudicatory power. Treating § 2409a(g) as nonjurisdictional better promotes fairness and access to justice in land-title disputes by allowing ordinary procedural rules (waiver/forfeiture and appropriate factual development) rather than mandatory dismissal under Rule 12(b)(1). The government’s interests in repose can still be fully protected by enforcing the statute of limitations on the merits without mislabeling it as a jurisdictional defect.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under this Court’s modern clear-statement rule, a statutory filing deadline is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly says so, and time bars are otherwise treated as nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules. Section 2409a(g) provides that “[a]ny civil action under” the QTA “shall be barred unless” brought within 12 years—language that reads like an ordinary statute of limitations and lacks a jurisdictional label or a placement in a jurisdiction-granting provision. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong holds that even deadlines attached to waivers of sovereign immunity are not automatically jurisdictional, so the government’s waiver-based argument cannot substitute for the required clear statement. Although Block v. North Dakota and United States v. Beggerly emphasize the QTA’s strict, compromise-based limits and the importance of repose in land-title disputes, those considerations go to the rigor of the time bar (and possibly tolling), not to whether it strips subject-matter jurisdiction absent clear jurisdictional text in § 2409a(g).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2409a(g) states that a quiet-title action “shall be barred” unless filed within 12 years, but it does not speak in jurisdictional terms (e.g., “no court shall have jurisdiction”), and under this Court’s clear-statement rule such time limits are presumptively nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong confirms that even in suits against the United States, a limitations period is not jurisdictional absent a clear congressional statement, and the mere fact that the deadline accompanies a waiver of sovereign immunity does not automatically transform it into a jurisdictional restriction. Treating the time bar as nonjurisdictional better respects separation of powers by keeping “jurisdiction” tethered to Congress’s clear words while leaving timeliness to ordinary litigation rules (waiver/forfeiture and merits-style pleading) unless Congress unmistakably provides otherwise. Whatever earlier-era assumptions suggested in cases like Mottaz, modern doctrine requires clarity in the text, and § 2409a(g) supplies none.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the Court’s modern clear-statement framework, statutory filing deadlines are presumptively nonjurisdictional unless Congress clearly states that the time bar limits the court’s subject-matter jurisdiction, and § 2409a(g) sets a 12-year deadline for bringing an action but does not speak in jurisdictional terms. Treating the QTA deadline as a claim-processing rule better accords with the Court’s post-Irwin approach to time bars in suits against the United States and avoids the practical and institutional costs of jurisdictional labeling (mandatory dismissal, no forfeiture, and distorted pleading standards) in land-title disputes. Any prior assumptions that sovereign-immunity conditions automatically entail jurisdiction have been narrowed by the Court’s more recent jurisdictionality cases, and stare decisis is not so entrenched here as to override the clear-statement rule. The Act’s structure still protects federal repose through a firm limitations defense, but without converting timeliness into a nonwaivable jurisdictional defect.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2409a(g) provides that a quiet-title “civil action under this section” must be “commenced within twelve years,” but it does not clearly state that the time bar limits the federal courts’ subject-matter jurisdiction; under this Court’s modern clear-statement rule, such deadlines are presumptively nonjurisdictional. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong, 575 U.S. 402 (2015), rejects the notion that a time limit becomes jurisdictional merely because it appears in a statute waiving sovereign immunity, and the QTA’s text lacks the jurisdictional “speak” Congress uses when it means to cabin adjudicatory power. Although Block v. North Dakota, 461 U.S. 273 (1983), used jurisdictional language about the QTA’s limit, Wong’s later methodological framework instructs courts to treat that kind of characterization as insufficient absent a clear jurisdictional statement in the statute itself. Accordingly, the 12-year deadline operates as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule, properly raised under Rule 12(b)(6) rather than Rule 12(b)(1).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2409a(g) states that a quiet-title action “shall be barred” unless brought within 12 years, but it does not clearly speak in jurisdictional terms or tie the deadline to the court’s adjudicatory power, and under the Court’s clear-statement rule time bars are presumptively nonjurisdictional. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong, 575 U.S. 402 (2015), makes clear that even limitations periods appearing in statutes waiving sovereign immunity are not jurisdictional absent a clear indication from Congress, and the QTA’s language looks like an ordinary statute of limitations rather than a jurisdictional grant or withdrawal. Treating § 2409a(g) as a claim-processing rule better promotes procedural fairness by allowing ordinary consequences like waiver/forfeiture and merits-style pleading under Rule 12(b)(6), without undermining the government’s repose interests because the time bar still applies when properly invoked. Older QTA cases like Block v. North Dakota and United States v. Mottaz should not be read to settle the jurisdictional label, particularly given the Court’s acknowledgment that it previously used “jurisdictional” imprecisely when discussing time prescriptions.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Quiet Title Act’s 12-year filing deadline is a jurisdictional limitation on federal courts (and thus nonwaivable and not subject to equitable doctrines) or a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g) (Quiet Title Act) (12-year deadline for bringing “[a]ny civil action under” the Act, except for actions brought by a State).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that § 2409a(g)’s 12-year deadline is not jurisdictional because Congress did not clearly state that the time bar limits the courts’ adjudicatory power; instead it functions like an ordinary statute of limitations (a claim-processing rule) that should be addressed under merits-style standards (e.g., Rule 12(b)(6)), can be forfeited or waived if not timely raised, and potentially allows equitable doctrines. They contend Ninth Circuit authority treating the deadline as jurisdictional rests on outdated assumptions about sovereign-immunity time limits and conflicts with the Supreme Court’s modern ‘clear statement’ approach to jurisdictionality.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues the 12-year deadline in § 2409a(g) is jurisdictional because the Quiet Title Act is a waiver of sovereign immunity and the deadline is a condition on that waiver; therefore, failure to sue within 12 years deprives the court of subject-matter jurisdiction and requires dismissal under Rule 12(b)(1). The government relies on prior Supreme Court and circuit precedent historically characterizing Quiet Title Act timeliness as a jurisdictional prerequisite, and emphasizes the need for predictable, firm limits on suits challenging federal title to land.
key_precedents: Tobar v. United States, 639 F.3d 1191 (9th Cir. 2011)
Maya v. Centex Corp., 658 F.3d 1060 (9th Cir. 2011)
Caltex Plastics, Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp., 824 F.3d 1156 (9th Cir. 2016)
Parrino v. FHP, Inc., 146 F.3d 699 (9th Cir. 1998)
Steinle v. City & County of San Francisco, 919 F.3d 1154 (9th Cir. 2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right that Block v. North Dakota repeatedly called § 2409a(g) a “condition on the waiver” and used the phrase “no jurisdiction,” and that sovereign-immunity waivers must be respected on their terms. But under our modern clear-statement framework—reinforced by United States v. Kwai Fun Wong—those earlier jurisdictional characterizations cannot do the work Congress did not do in the statutory text, and § 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless” is classic limitations language not tied to adjudicatory power. Stare decisis matters, yet reading Block as controlling on the label would freeze an older, since-disavowed conflation of waiver-conditions with jurisdiction, rather than applying today’s jurisdictionality doctrine to the statute as written. A narrow holding that § 2409a(g) is nonjurisdictional—but still a strict, mandatory time bar when the Government properly raises it—best preserves repose without expanding sua sponte jurisdictional dismissals.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan rely on Kwai Fun Wong’s clear-statement framework, but that modern atextual presumption cannot override the original public meaning of § 2409a(g)’s terms of consent: an action “under this section … shall be barred unless” timely filed, which defines when the United States has agreed to be sued at all. Justice Gorsuch is right that the text uses familiar limitations language, yet in a sovereign-immunity waiver the relevant question is whether Congress conditioned its consent—not whether it used the word “jurisdiction”—and Block v. North Dakota squarely held this very provision is such a condition leaving courts with “no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits” once the period runs. Wong, as a general time-bar case, does not supply textual authority to add equitable exceptions or waiver to the QTA’s carefully delimited cause of action, especially given the Act’s central aim of repose for federal title. I therefore remain with Justice Alito that Block’s QTA-specific holding and the statute’s conditional phrasing control over an abstract clear-statement gloss untethered from what Congress enacted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the modern clear-statement framework of Kwai Fun Wong and the absence of the word “jurisdiction” in § 2409a(g), but that focus is too narrow for this statute’s structure: the Quiet Title Act is the waiver itself, and § 2409a(g) defines when an action may be brought “under this section,” which reads most naturally as a condition on the Government’s consent rather than a freestanding claims-processing rule. Block v. North Dakota is not merely an older “labeling” case; as Justice Thomas stresses, it squarely treated the 12-year bar as delimiting the scope of the waiver and stated that after the period runs courts have “no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits,” a QTA-specific holding I do not read Wong as silently displacing. Even if Wong rejects a categorical sovereign-immunity presumption, it does not require us to ignore Congress’s evident aim of finality in federal land titles, which is best served by a nonwaivable boundary on suit rather than a defense susceptible to forfeiture. In my view, the opposing side’s approach effectively rewrites the terms of consent Congress enacted, and I am not persuaded that the clear-statement cases compel that result in this particular statutory setting.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press their strongest point: Block’s statement that once § 2409a(g) runs the court has “no jurisdiction,” and the traditional idea that conditions on a sovereign-immunity waiver delimit judicial power. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Kwai Fun Wong rejects treating a limitations period as jurisdictional merely because it appears in a waiver, and our clear-statement cases do not let earlier judicial characterizations supply the jurisdictional consequences Congress did not clearly enact. The text here—“shall be barred unless”—reads like an ordinary, mandatory time bar, not a limit on adjudicatory power, so repose and title stability can be fully protected through a limitations defense without the harsh, sua sponte, nonwaivable effects that particularly burden less-resourced landowners. Block remains relevant to enforcing the deadline strictly when raised, but it cannot, under modern doctrine, substitute for the missing jurisdictional hook in the statute’s text.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is Block’s explicit statement that once the QTA period runs, courts have “no jurisdiction,” coupled with the traditional view that conditions on sovereign-immunity waivers delimit jurisdiction. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, Kwai Fun Wong rejects the premise that sovereign-immunity context automatically makes a time bar jurisdictional, and our clear-statement framework requires Congress to link the deadline to adjudicatory power in the statutory text—something § 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless commenced” does not do. I read Block’s jurisdictional rhetoric as pre-Wong shorthand for a strict, non-equitable limitations rule rather than a holding that Congress clearly made this a nonwaivable Rule 12(b)(1) defect. Treating § 2409a(g) as nonjurisdictional still fully protects repose when the Government raises the defense, while avoiding the modernly disfavored consequences of jurisdictional labeling absent a textual hook.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is Block’s repeated description of § 2409a(g) as a “condition on the waiver” that leaves courts with “no jurisdiction,” invoking the traditional maxim that consent-to-suit terms define jurisdiction. But under the modern clear-statement rule articulated in Kwai Fun Wong—an approach Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett rightly emphasize—we look to whether Congress clearly tied the time bar to the court’s adjudicatory power, and § 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless commenced within twelve years” reads as classic limitations language, not a jurisdictional withdrawal. Block’s jurisdictional label, issued before our current framework, cannot supply the missing statutory text; at most it confirms the deadline’s strict enforceability when properly raised. Justice Alito’s repose concerns remain weighty, but they are satisfied by treating the provision as a mandatory limitations defense without converting it into a nonwaivable Rule 12(b)(1) defect.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas press the strongest point: Block’s repeated description of § 2409a(g) as a “condition on the waiver” and its statement that courts have “no jurisdiction” once the period runs. But under our institutional, text-first clear-statement framework—highlighted by the Chief Justice and reinforced by Kwai Fun Wong—older jurisdictional labels in precedent cannot substitute for Congress clearly linking a deadline to adjudicatory power, and § 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless” is standard limitations language rather than a jurisdictional withdrawal. Stare decisis still matters, so Block remains important for the strict enforcement of the 12-year bar when properly raised, but it does not control the jurisdictional characterization after Wong’s rejection of the sovereign-immunity-equals-jurisdiction premise. This approach preserves the Government’s strong repose interests without the legitimacy and fairness costs of mandatory sua sponte jurisdictional dismissals.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that, in the sovereign-immunity setting, § 2409a(g) can be read as a condition on the Government’s consent, and Block used “no jurisdiction” language. But under the Court’s modern, text-centered clear-statement framework—applied in United States v. Kwai Fun Wong—those older jurisdictional characterizations cannot do the work Congress did not do in the statute’s text, and “shall be barred unless” is ordinary limitations phrasing not tied to adjudicatory power. Justice Alito’s stare decisis and repose concerns are substantial, yet they are satisfied by strict enforcement as a mandatory limitations defense when raised, without importing the nonwaivable, sua sponte consequences that our current doctrine reserves for unmistakably jurisdictional provisions. On my methodology, Block is best read as reflecting the pre-Wong linkage between waiver conditions and jurisdiction rather than a controlling interpretation of § 2409a(g)’s text as jurisdictional.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito most forcefully press Block v. North Dakota’s description of § 2409a(g) as a “condition on the waiver” and its statement that courts have “no jurisdiction” after 12 years, but under our modern clear-statement approach those judicial labels cannot substitute for Congress expressly linking timeliness to adjudicatory power. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 2409a(g)’s “shall be barred unless” reads like ordinary limitations language and contains no jurisdictional terms or placement that would do the “something special” our cases require. Alito’s repose/finality concerns are real, but they are fully served by a strict, mandatory (yet waivable/forfeitable) limitations defense, without the procedural harshness and sua sponte dismissals that disproportionately undermine fairness in close or under-resourced cases. Block remains relevant to the strictness of the deadline when properly invoked, but Wong undercuts treating sovereign-immunity time bars as categorically jurisdictional absent a clear statutory statement.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2409a(g) provides that a quiet-title action “shall be barred unless it is commenced within twelve years,” but it does not “speak in jurisdictional terms” or refer to the district courts’ adjudicatory power, which under the Court’s clear-statement approach is ordinarily required to treat a deadline as jurisdictional. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong, 575 U.S. 402 (2015), makes clear that a time bar is not jurisdictional merely because it appears in a waiver of sovereign immunity; Congress must do “something special” to attach jurisdictional consequences. Treating the QTA deadline as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule respects that modern framework while allowing the government to prevail on timeliness through ordinary merits procedures if it properly raises the defense. In the absence of a clear jurisdictional statement in § 2409a(g), I would avoid expanding jurisdictional dismissals and decide narrowly that the limitation is nonjurisdictional.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Quiet Title Act’s waiver of sovereign immunity is strictly limited by the terms Congress enacted, and § 2409a(g) provides that “[a]ny civil action under this section” is barred unless commenced within 12 years of accrual—text that operates as a condition on the waiver rather than a mere claims-processing rule. In Block v. North Dakota, 461 U.S. 273, 287–88, 292 (1983), this Court treated the 12-year limitation as a jurisdictional prerequisite, explaining that the “limitations provision constitutes a condition on the waiver of sovereign immunity” and that when a suit is barred by § 2409a(g) the court has “no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits.” Under the original understanding of sovereign immunity and this Court’s longstanding rule that “the terms of [the United States’] consent to be sued … define [the] court’s jurisdiction,” Lehman v. Nakshian, 453 U.S. 156, 160 (1981), the filing deadline is nonwaivable and not subject to equitable doctrines absent clear textual authorization. Accordingly, failure to sue within the 12-year period deprives federal courts of subject-matter jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2409a(g) provides that “[a]ny civil action under this section” is barred unless brought within 12 years, and because the Quiet Title Act is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity, that deadline is best read as a condition on the waiver rather than an ordinary, waivable claim-processing rule. In Block v. North Dakota, 461 U.S. 273, 292 (1983), the Court treated the QTA’s time bar as jurisdictional, stating that if the limitations period had run “the courts below had no jurisdiction to inquire into the merits,” and that controlling characterization should govern absent a clear overruling. Treating the deadline as jurisdictional also serves the practical consequences Congress likely sought—finality and predictability for federal land title and reduced disruption to governmental land management from stale claims. Accordingly, an untimely QTA suit must be dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction and is not subject to waiver or equitable tolling.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under this Court’s modern “clear statement” rule, a filing deadline is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly says it limits the courts’ adjudicatory power; § 2409a(g) sets a 12-year deadline but does not speak in jurisdictional terms. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong holds that “it makes no difference that a time bar conditions a waiver of sovereign immunity,” rejecting the government’s argument that such limits are automatically jurisdictional, and instead treats such deadlines as ordinary claim-processing rules absent a clear jurisdictional tag. Although Block v. North Dakota used jurisdictional language about the Quiet Title Act’s limitations period, that phrasing reflects an earlier sovereign-immunity approach that Wong expressly disavows, and it should not foreclose applying the clear-statement framework here. Treating § 2409a(g) as nonjurisdictional better serves fairness and access to justice by permitting waiver/forfeiture and (where warranted) equitable doctrines for landowners who may otherwise be shut out on technical grounds.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2409a(g) sets a 12-year deadline for bringing an action under the Quiet Title Act, but it does not clearly speak in jurisdictional terms or tie the time bar to the courts’ adjudicatory power, which under the Court’s modern clear-statement framework points to a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong, 575 U.S. 402 (2015), specifically rejects the idea that a limitations period is jurisdictional simply because it appears in a statute waiving sovereign immunity, and § 2409a(g)’s text likewise reads like an ordinary statute of limitations. Treating the deadline as nonjurisdictional promotes workability by channeling timeliness disputes into ordinary merits procedures (and allowing waiver/forfeiture), while still honoring Congress’s evident purpose of repose through enforcement when properly raised. Any prior characterizations of the QTA deadline as “jurisdictional” should not control absent a clear jurisdictional statement in § 2409a(g), consistent with the Court’s current jurisdictionality doctrine.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2409a(g) sets a 12-year deadline for bringing an action under the Quiet Title Act, but it does not clearly state that the time bar limits the federal courts’ adjudicatory power or speaks in jurisdictional terms; under the Court’s modern clear-statement rule, that is decisive. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong holds that even in waivers of sovereign immunity, a limitations period is not jurisdictional absent a clear congressional statement, and Congress must do “something special” beyond an exception-free deadline to make it so. Treating § 2409a(g) as nonjurisdictional respects the separation between merits rules and jurisdiction, leaving timeliness to ordinary litigation mechanisms (waiver/forfeiture and, where appropriate, equitable doctrines) rather than Rule 12(b)(1). Prior characterizations of QTA timeliness as “jurisdictional” rest on an older sovereign-immunity presumption Wong rejected and cannot overcome the statute’s text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 2409a(g) sets a 12-year time limit for bringing an action under the Quiet Title Act, but it does not clearly state that the deadline limits the federal courts’ subject-matter jurisdiction; under this Court’s modern clear-statement approach, that makes it a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong held that statutory time bars in suits against the United States are not automatically jurisdictional merely because they accompany a sovereign-immunity waiver, and nothing in § 2409a(g)’s text uses the kind of jurisdictional language this Court requires. Although older cases characterized similar limits as jurisdictional in an “earlier era,” stare decisis is best respected by following the Court’s current jurisdictionality framework while leaving the government fully able to raise timeliness as an affirmative defense. Treating the deadline as nonjurisdictional also promotes practical workability by channeling disputes into ordinary merits procedures (e.g., Rule 12(b)(6)) without expanding judicial power beyond Congress’s clear instruction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2409a(g) provides that a quiet-title action "shall be barred" unless commenced within 12 years, language that reads as an ordinary limitations defense rather than a clear restriction on a federal court’s adjudicatory power. Under this Court’s modern textual clear-statement rule, time bars are not jurisdictional absent unmistakable jurisdictional language, and that approach applies even in waivers of sovereign immunity. United States v. Kwai Fun Wong rejected the premise that limitations periods are jurisdictional merely because they accompany a sovereign-immunity waiver, and nothing in § 2409a(g)’s text clearly links timeliness to subject-matter jurisdiction. Prior characterizations in cases like Block v. North Dakota and United States v. Mottaz are best read as reflecting an earlier, now-disfavored methodology, and in any event do not supply the requisite clear statement in the statute’s text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2409a(g) sets a 12-year deadline for bringing an action “under” the Quiet Title Act, but it does not clearly state that untimeliness strips federal courts of adjudicatory power, as required by this Court’s clear-statement framework for jurisdictionality. Under United States v. Kwai Fun Wong, “it makes no difference” to the jurisdictional inquiry that the time bar appears in a sovereign-immunity waiver; absent a clear statement, filing deadlines are treated as nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules subject to waiver/forfeiture and potentially equitable doctrines. The Act’s text is a classic limitations provision rather than a jurisdiction-conferring clause, and treating it as nonjurisdictional better promotes procedural fairness by allowing ordinary merits-style litigation rules (e.g., Rule 12(b)(6)) rather than mandatory sua sponte dismissal under Rule 12(b)(1). The government’s reliance on historical characterizations cannot overcome Wong’s directive to examine text, context, and history for a clear jurisdictional statement, and Beggerly’s engagement with tolling considerations is more consistent with a nonjurisdictional limitations rule than a rigid jurisdictional bar.
